strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: automatically selecting distributed training strategies across PP, DP, TP, and FSDP can reduce expert tuning effort for large model training.

The high-level idea of jointly optimizing inter-layer placement and intra-layer strategy choices is sensible, and the paper gives a reasonably clear end-to-end pipeline with profiling, cost modeling, optimization, and execution.

The evaluation includes actual training throughput measurements rather than only simulator results, with several transformer models and multiple hardware environments, including ViT and Swin as computer vision cases.
The ablation constraining the search space to inter-layer-only or intra-layer-only choices supports the qualitative claim that a larger joint strategy space can matter.
weaknesses: The central MIQP formulation appears technically underspecified or incorrect as written. Equations such as the computation-stage and communication-stage constraints multiply layer-placement variables with a bilinear strategy-cost term, yielding higher-order products rather than a standard mixed-integer quadratic program. The paper does not explain a valid linearization/quadratization or implementation mapping to Gurobi, which directly undermines the main technical claim.

The repeated claim of finding an “optimal solution” is not supported. The objective depends on approximate cost models, and Appendix E uses a 60s Gurobi time limit plus early stopping at up to a 4% gap, so the method is not guaranteed to return a proven optimum even for its own model.

The cost model relies on simplifying assumptions that are only partially validated: backward time is approximated as twice forward time, optimizer/update costs are ignored, memory modeling is coarse for pipeline schedules, and estimation accuracy is reported only in a limited setting. These approximations are material because the method’s ranking of strategies depends on them.

The experimental evidence is weaker than the headline claims suggest. On ENVA, UniAP often matches Galvatron rather than improving throughput; on ENVB it is slightly worse on T5; on ENVD it matches Megatron throughput and improves only search time. Several comparisons rely on failed, unsupported, or out-of-memory baselines, making the reported maximum speedups less convincing.

Reproducibility is limited. The strategy dictionary, solver reformulation, profiling overhead, execution-plan generation, and full implementation details are not sufficiently specified, and the dependence on a commercial Gurobi solver further complicates independent reproduction.

The baseline comparison is not fully fair or diagnostic. Optimization time excludes profiling, Gurobi is allowed multithreaded commercial solving while dynamic-programming baselines are described as single-threaded, and Alpa comparisons are often unavailable or fail due to implementation issues rather than demonstrated inferiority.

The paper’s contribution to computer vision is indirect. Most of the technical contribution is a distributed training systems method for transformers in general, with only ViT and Swin as CV examples and no evaluation on broader CV workloads such as detection, segmentation, CNNs, or modern large-scale vision-language training.

The scalability evidence is limited: the main node-scaling experiments also scale the batch size, so they primarily show weak scaling rather than strong scaling or robustness under fixed workload constraints.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: automatically choosing distributed training strategies across pipeline, data, tensor, and fully sharded data parallelism. This is useful for large-scale model training, including vision transformers.

The unified MIQP formulation is a coherent attempt to couple inter-layer placement with intra-layer strategy selection, rather than optimizing them hierarchically. The notation, constraints, and appendices make the intended optimization problem mostly understandable.

The experimental section covers multiple models and hardware environments, including ViT/Swin and large language models, and reports both training throughput and strategy optimization time. Some results are compelling, especially on ENVB and the Llama-7B ENVC case versus Galvatron.

The paper includes useful supporting analyses: scalability experiments, an ablation of inter-layer-only/intra-layer-only search spaces, cost-model estimation error, and a concrete BERT-Huge strategy case study.
weaknesses: The central claim of finding an “optimal solution” is overstated. The guarantee is only with respect to an approximate cost model and a constrained strategy dictionary, while the solver is run with time limits and early stopping. This is not the same as guaranteeing the fastest real training strategy.

The complexity analysis is misleading: treating the MIQP solver time limit as a constant hides the NP-hardness and trades optimality for bounded runtime. This directly conflicts with the paper’s repeated optimality claims.

The cost model is simplified and only partially validated. It assumes backward time is roughly twice forward time, uses profiled communication efficiencies and overlap coefficients, and models GPipe-style execution with a compact formula. The reported 3.59% estimation error is encouraging, but appears limited and does not establish robustness across the full search space, all hardware, or all candidate strategies.

The evaluation has several fairness and completeness issues. Many baseline entries are MEM/CUDA/N/A/SOL rather than successful comparisons; Alpa is unavailable for Swin-Huge and Llama; ENVD comparisons are against manual Megatron/DeepSpeed rather than comparable AP systems; and some headline gains come from baseline failure or incomplete support. On ENVA, UniAP matches Galvatron on three models rather than improving throughput, and on T5-Large ENVB it is slightly worse.

The strategy optimization time comparison is not fully convincing. It is unclear whether profiling overhead is included, and comparing UniAP’s solver time against manual or framework-specific baseline search procedures may not isolate the method’s intrinsic planning efficiency.

Reproducibility is weak. I found no code release or artifact statement, and the method depends on detailed profiling, hardware topology, framework integrations, Gurobi, adapted DCU libraries, and a largely unspecified strategy dictionary. These are substantial barriers to reproducing the reported results.

The contribution is only indirectly connected to computer vision and pattern recognition. Although ViT and Swin are evaluated, the method is fundamentally a distributed training systems contribution rather than a vision-method contribution, making the CVPR fit questionable.

Several important scope limitations are underdeveloped: heterogeneous clusters are left for future work despite being invoked as motivation, only Transformer-style models are evaluated, activation checkpointing is disabled, and the main formulation is illustrated for GPipe with limited evidence for other pipeline schedules.

weaknesses: A central technical issue is that the stated MIQP formulation appears under-specified: constraints such as the intra-stage and cross-stage resharding costs contain products of layer-placement variables and two strategy-selection variables, which are higher-order than quadratic as written. strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: automatically choosing distributed training strategies across pipeline, data, tensor, and sharded data parallelism. A unified search over inter-layer and intra-layer strategies is a useful direction, especially for large Transformer training.

The manuscript gives a reasonably clear high-level workflow, defines cost and memory models, and includes a mathematical formulation with placement, strategy-selection, memory, and order-preserving constraints.

The experiments cover several hardware settings and model families, including BERT, T5, ViT, Swin, and Llama. Some reported gains are meaningful, especially the ENVB and ENVC cases where UniAP finds higher-throughput strategies than Galvatron/Alpa and substantially reduces planning time.
The appendix adds useful details, including Gurobi settings, model configurations, cost-estimation error, and a concrete case study illustrating the mixed PP/DP/TP/FSDP strategy found by UniAP.
weaknesses: The central technical claim that the method is an MIQP and finds an optimal solution is not adequately supported. Several constraints as written include products such as Pui Pvi times Su^T Ruv Sv, which appear quartic in binary variables rather than quadratic. The paper does not show a valid linearization/quadratization or explain how these expressions are passed to the solver.

The optimality claims are overstated. The implementation uses a 60-second Gurobi time limit and early stopping with a relaxed gap condition, so the returned strategy is not necessarily globally optimal even for the stated cost model. In addition, the cost model is approximate, so optimality in the modeled objective does not imply optimal training throughput.

The complexity analysis is misleading: treating the MIQP solver time limit as a constant hides the intrinsic hardness of the optimization problem and does not characterize solution quality or scaling of the solver. This weakens the methodological evidence substantially.

The evaluation is suggestive but not decisive. UniAP ties Galvatron on several ENVA cases, is slightly worse on T5-Large in ENVB, and several baseline entries are unavailable, fail with OOM, or rely on implementation failures rather than complete comparisons. The largest 3.80x throughput gain is against Galvatron only, with Alpa unavailable.

The baseline comparison is not fully controlled. Alpa is marked N/A for Swin and Llama due to compilation/adaptation issues, DeepSpeed fails because of a divisibility constraint in one setup, and the Megatron comparison emphasizes manual search time rather than a strong tuned baseline.

Reproducibility is limited. The method depends on Gurobi, a proprietary solver, and the paper does not provide enough detail on the strategy dictionary, profiling procedure, solver formulation after any product transformations, or baseline adaptation to independently reproduce the main results.

The contribution is mostly distributed training systems rather than computer vision or pattern recognition. The inclusion of ViT and Swin experiments gives some CV relevance, but the paper does not advance vision modeling, representation learning, or recognition methodology directly.

Some modeling assumptions are narrow: GPipe-style scheduling is used for illustration, activation checkpointing is disabled, heterogeneous clusters are left as future work despite being motivated, and the cost model uses simplified backward/forward timing and overlap assumptions that may not hold broadly.

The unified optimization framing is appealing, and the manuscript gives a reasonably clear end-to-end pipeline with profiling, cost modeling, placement constraints, memory constraints, and an order-preserving proof in the appendix.

Some results are compelling: UniAP improves throughput on ENVB for BERT/ViT/Swin, achieves a reported 3.80x throughput gain over Galvatron for Llama-7B on ENVC, and substantially reduces optimization time in many settings.
The ablation comparing inter-layer-only, intra-layer-only, and unified strategy spaces supports the central intuition that joint strategy selection can avoid infeasible or suboptimal configurations.
weaknesses: The claimed MIQP formulation is not fully specified and appears technically problematic as written. Equations such as the intra-stage and cross-stage resharding terms multiply placement variables with quadratic strategy-selection terms, yielding higher-order products rather than a standard MIQP unless additional auxiliary variables and linearization are introduced. The max term in the objective is also not explicitly reformulated. This weakens confidence in the central technical claim.

The paper repeatedly claims to find an optimal strategy, but the optimality is only with respect to an estimated cost model, a restricted strategy dictionary, enumerated pipeline/microbatch factors, and a solver configuration that includes early stopping with up to a 4% gap. The experimental comparisons are useful but uneven. Several baselines are unavailable, fail to compile, run out of memory, or have no solution; on ENVA UniAP ties Galvatron on three models, and on ENVD it matches Megatron throughput rather than improving it. weaknesses: The central technical claim is overstated. The formulation is presented as MIQP, but several constraints as written contain products such as Pui Pvi (Su^T Ruv Sv), which are quartic in binary variables unless additional linearization or lifted variables are introduced. Those transformations are not specified, making the claimed MIQP formulation and reproducibility questionable.

The claim of finding an optimal solution is not adequately supported. The method optimizes an approximate cost model, enumerates a restricted set of pipeline sizes and micro-batch counts, and uses Gurobi with a 60 second limit plus early stopping at up to 4% MIP gap. This supports finding good strategies, but not guaranteed globally optimal training throughput.

The order-preserving constraint appears insufficient as stated: requiring each stage subgraph to be contiguous does not by itself enforce that pipeline stage indices follow the graph topological order. A reversed or permuted stage labeling can still be contiguous, while cross-stage communication costs are only modeled for j to j+1 transitions.

The CV contribution is indirect. Only ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge are vision models, and the work is mainly a distributed training systems paper with no evaluation on detection, segmentation, diffusion, video, or downstream vision accuracy. Its fit to CVPR is therefore weaker than to ML systems venues.

The empirical evidence has fairness and coverage limitations. Several baseline entries are MEM/CUDA/N/A or capped at >40 minutes, Alpa is missing for Swin and Llama due to implementation issues, and the DCU experiments compare mainly to manual Megatron/DeepSpeed rather than similarly capable AP systems. Some headline settings are ties or slight regressions, such as T5 on ENVB-8.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the strategy dictionary/search space, exact solver formulation after any linearization, profiling overhead, software versions, and baseline tuning details are not sufficiently specified. The reliance on commercial Gurobi also raises practical reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important systems problem: automatically choosing combinations of pipeline, data, tensor, and FSDP parallelism for large-model training. A unified optimizer over inter- and intra-layer choices is potentially useful.
The manuscript gives a reasonably concrete formulation with placement variables, strategy-selection variables, memory constraints, contiguity constraints, and a profiling-based cost model.
The evaluation uses measured training throughput, not only simulation, across several hardware environments and several Transformer models, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge.

Some reported results are practically meaningful, especially the ENVB improvements over Galvatron/Alpa and the ENVC Llama-7B case, and the paper also reports optimization time, scalability, estimation error, an ablation, and a case study.
weaknesses: The core technical claim that the formulation is MIQP is not adequately supported. Equations such as the resharding terms contain products like P_ui P_vi (S_u^T R_uv S_v), which expand to higher-order products of binary variables, and the max term in the objective also needs an explicit reformulation. No linearization or auxiliary-variable construction is given, so the solver formulation is incomplete as written.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal solution is overstated. The method optimizes an approximate profiled cost model, assumes BP time is roughly twice FP time, omits optimizer-step cost, depends on a fixed and insufficiently specified strategy dictionary, and in Appendix E uses time limits and early stopping at up to 4% MIP gap, which does not guarantee global optimality.

The contribution is not well aligned with CVPR as a computer vision or pattern recognition paper. The work is primarily a distributed training systems paper; only two evaluated models are vision models, and the paper does not study vision accuracy, convergence behavior, downstream visual recognition impact, or vision-specific modeling issues.

The empirical comparison is uneven. Many baseline entries are N/A, OOM, MEM, compilation failure, or no-solution cases, and several headline gains rely on those failures or on a single Llama setting. In multiple reported settings UniAP matches Galvatron exactly or is slightly worse, e.g. ENVA BERT/T5/ViT, ENVB T5, and ENVD throughput.

The manual-parallelism comparison is not convincing. Treating Megatron strategy optimization as a long exhaustive/manual search and arguing that users choose strategies randomly does not establish superiority over expert-tuned manual baselines under fair effort or realistic tuning protocols.

Reproducibility is limited. The exact strategy space, profiling procedure, implementation details, software versions, topology handling, and baseline adaptation details are not sufficiently specified, and the method depends on commercial Gurobi. The paper also omits some training hyperparameters, saying they minimally affect throughput, but they can still affect memory and execution behavior.

The complexity analysis is misleading because it treats MIQP solver time as a constant due to a time limit, while the underlying optimization is combinatorial and solution quality then depends on early termination. This weakens the scalability claim beyond the tested cases.

Clarity is adequate at a high level but rough in important places: notation is dense, several claims are phrased too absolutely, limitations are minimal, and there are presentation issues and typos. These are secondary to the technical and evidential concerns above.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: automatically choosing combined pipeline, data, tensor, and FSDP strategies for distributed training. The central idea of jointly optimizing inter-layer and intra-layer parallelism is useful and well motivated against hierarchical planners.

The manuscript provides a concrete optimization framework with profiling, time/memory cost models, constraints for placement, strategy selection, memory, and order preservation, plus an algorithmic description and appendices that improve readability.

The empirical section is reasonably broad for a systems paper: it covers multiple Transformer-style NLP and vision models, several hardware environments including V100, TITAN Xp, A100, and DCU clusters, and reports both training throughput and strategy optimization time.

The reported results support practical value in several cases: UniAP matches the best baseline when the same strategy is found, improves throughput substantially on ENVB and Llama-7B on ENVC, finds feasible strategies where some baselines fail, and reduces search time markedly.

The paper includes useful supporting analyses, including scalability experiments, an ablation contrasting inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only spaces, cost-model estimation error, and a case study of the selected BERT-Huge strategy.
weaknesses: A key technical concern is that the optimization is not clearly an MIQP as written. Equations involving Pui Pvi (S_u^T R_uv S_v) appear higher than quadratic in binary variables, and the max term in the objective also requires auxiliary-variable linearization. The paper does not explain the reformulation actually passed to Gurobi, which weakens the technical correctness and reproducibility of the main formulation.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal strategy is stronger than the evidence supports. Appendix E sets a 60s Gurobi time limit and includes early stopping at a 4% optimality gap, so the solved problem may be approximate; additionally, the cost model itself is an approximation. The paper should distinguish solver optimality, modeled-cost optimality, and measured-throughput optimality.

The evaluation is strong in places but uneven. Several Alpa comparisons are N/A or fail due to implementation/compilation issues, Galvatron fails in some cases, and the largest reported throughput gain lacks a comparable Alpa result. Table 2 shows UniAP and Megatron achieving identical throughput, so the advantage there is search time rather than a better training strategy.

The method is evaluated almost entirely on Transformer-family workloads. Although ViT and Swin provide a CV connection, the contribution is primarily distributed training systems rather than computer vision methodology, and there is no evaluation on broader CV workloads such as CNNs, detection, segmentation, or multimodal models.

Important practical features are simplified or omitted: activation checkpointing is turned off, the objective excludes optimizer update time, GPipe is the main pipeline schedule, and integration with modern memory-saving and scheduling techniques is not evaluated. These choices may limit applicability to contemporary large-scale training practice.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives hardware, model, batch-size, and some Gurobi details, but exact code, profiling protocol, strategy dictionaries, software versions, baseline adaptation details, and scripts for the specialized DCU environment are not provided in the manuscript. The reliance on a commercial solver also affects reproducibility.

Some presentation issues remain: the paper says five Transformer-based models while the appendix lists six, there are minor typos, and some baseline failure modes such as MEM, SOL, CUDA, and N/A would benefit from more precise diagnostic explanation. These are not fatal but add friction.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: automatic selection of distributed training strategies across pipeline, data, tensor, and fully sharded data parallelism. Jointly optimizing inter-layer and intra-layer choices is a meaningful contribution over hierarchical search schemes.

The MIQP/UOP framing is conceptually elegant and useful: it gives a unified way to express placement, strategy selection, memory constraints, communication costs, and pipeline costs, rather than stitching together separate optimizers.
The experimental evidence is fairly broad for a systems paper: results cover BERT, T5, ViT, Swin, and Llama-family models on several hardware environments, including NVIDIA GPUs and DCU clusters.

Reported results are compelling in several settings, especially the 3.80x Llama-7B throughput gain over Galvatron on ENVC and large reductions in strategy optimization time, while also matching strong baselines in cases where the same optimal strategy is found.

The paper includes useful supporting analysis: scalability studies, an ablation contrasting joint optimization with inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only search, cost-model error analysis, and a concrete case study of the selected strategy.
weaknesses: The strongest technical claim, that UniAP finds an optimal solution, is overstated. The result is optimal only with respect to the profiled cost model, enumerated pipeline sizes/micro-batch choices, and solver settings; the appendix also uses time limits and early stopping, so exact MIQP optimality is not always guaranteed.

The mathematical formulation as written is not clearly an MIQP: terms such as Pui Pvi (Su^T Ruv Sv) appear higher than quadratic in binary variables unless additional auxiliary variables or linearization are introduced. This weakens technical clarity and reproducibility of the core method.

The evaluation is strong but uneven. Several baselines are missing, fail, or are marked N/A in important settings; on ENVA UniAP often matches rather than improves over Galvatron, and on ENVB T5-Large it is slightly worse. The headline speedups therefore describe selected cases rather than uniform superiority.

The work is more of a distributed ML systems contribution than a computer vision contribution. The inclusion of ViT/Swin experiments helps, but the method is not vision-specific and its CVPR relevance depends mainly on efficient training utility.

Reproducibility has some friction: the approach depends on Gurobi, profiling details are not fully specified, and implementation availability is not discussed. Reproducing the full hardware-dependent comparison would be difficult without substantial engineering effort.
